messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 80
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Coast Guard
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 64

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened, Future Orientation: Talking about the future, Auditory (Sirens): Sirens
  Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Thinking: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad, Positive Reframing: I force myself to think only positive thoughts, Thought Suppression: I try to push them out of my mind
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
  Negative Appraisals: Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Harjit Singh is an 80-year-old widowed Coast Guard veteran who still works in a reduced civilian support role near the harbor, and he dates the beginning of his trouble to an accident several years ago during a shoreline rescue exercise in a wooded coastal area. A younger crewman was moving equipment down a steep, brush-covered embankment while Harjit directed the team. There had been sirens from emergency vehicles on the access road above, gulls, surf, and shouted orders crossing over each other. Harjit gave a command too quickly, and the crewman lost his footing, tumbling onto rocks below and sustaining devastating injuries. Harjit remembers seeing the man’s body twisted among wet branches and hearing the sirens continue as if nothing had happened. Ever since, natural settings resembling that stretch of coast—tree line, damp earth, salt air—have carried a terrible charge for him, and even routine talk about “next year” or retirement can land with the force of accusation, because the future is precisely what he feels he damaged for another man.

What stays with him is not a continuous memory but a broken set of pieces. When he tries to recall the event on purpose, he says his mind “goes blank where it matters,” yet at other times the whole scene returns with overpowering vividness: the smell of mud and seawater, the rising sirens, the sight of brush shaking where the man fell. Because these fragments arrive disconnected and then suddenly all at once, he has grown increasingly sensitive to cues around him. A siren on the street outside the station, a path through coastal scrub, even conversation about upcoming plans can pull the memory forward before he knows what is happening. He has come to dread those moments not only because they are distressing, but because they seem to prove to him that the event is still lodged in him in some dangerous, unfinished way.

Over time Harjit has come to believe the accident happened because of the kind of man he is. He does not describe himself as having made a mistake so much as being fundamentally flawed, “the sort of person who ruins things.” That belief has made him scan constantly for danger, as if letting down his guard would expose more of this defect. In unfamiliar places he becomes uneasy because he cannot quickly map exits, hazards, or where people are standing. At meetings he quietly chooses the seat that feels most protected, usually with a wall behind him and a clear line to the door. When he feels keyed up in this way, the world itself seems to fill with reminders: the wail of an ambulance becomes unbearable, and if someone at work starts discussing future staffing or long-term plans, he feels a jolt of shame, as though he has no right to imagine a future after costing someone else so much.

His response has been to fight his own mind. He tells himself the incident was not really as bad as he remembers, or that perhaps he has exaggerated its seriousness over the years. At other times he forces himself into bright, corrective thoughts—telling himself to focus only on blessings, to think positively, to stop dwelling. Most often he tries to push the images away the instant they begin. These efforts make sense to him because they are driven by a desperate wish not to be the kind of man he fears he is. Yet the more firmly he suppresses the scene or insists it was not real, the less coherent his memory becomes when he tries to approach it deliberately, and the more violently it seems to return through sirens, shoreline brush, or casual talk of the future. Afterward he is left feeling even more disturbed by himself, as if only a defective person would need to deny something so grave.

The cycle has tightened in his daily life. At the harbor he avoids unfamiliar assignments and dislikes going to new locations unless he has studied them in advance. Even on ordinary errands he scans for the safest chair in a diner or waiting room. He has also become more reckless in smaller, unsettling ways, taking physical risks he dismisses with a shrug, as though his own safety matters less than it used to. Those moments are followed by a grim self-recognition that deepens his self-blame. When he has spent a day on edge, his memory is more likely to break through in full sensory form that night; when that happens, he doubles down on pushing it out of mind the next day, which leaves him even more reactive to the next siren or stand of trees. Since his wife died, there is no one at home to interrupt this pattern, and his world has narrowed around routes and settings he feels he can control.

He finally sought help after freezing during a planning conversation at work about next season’s training schedule. Someone mentioned the future of the unit, a siren sounded outside, and he was abruptly back on that embankment, smelling wet earth and hearing his own command. He had to leave the room and later sat in his truck shaken and ashamed, convinced his mind was failing and that he was still dangerous to others. What he fears most is not simply remembering, but confirming his belief that there is something rotten in his character. What he hopes, though he says this cautiously, is to understand why the past still arrives as if it is happening now and whether he can live whatever years remain without bracing against every sound, every landscape, and every mention of what comes next.
